diagnostic_evidence.quote: We also adopt the convention that $\operatorname{dist}(0, \emptyset) = \infty$.

issues.failure_explanation: Assumption (iii) requires the KL inequality for every x in the open set Ω, which strictly contains 𝒳=dom p. For x∈Ω\𝒳 we have ∂p(x)=∅, so ∂Ψ(x)=∅ and dist(0,∂Ψ(x))=∞. Then 𝓛(x)={y: 0<F*(x)-F(x,y)} is the whole non-optimal region, so the full global KL inequality is required at such x. In the Example, take x slightly above 2 (inside any open Ω ⊃ [1,2]) and y=π. There the y-gradient is zero and the normal cone is [0,∞), so dist(0,∇_yφ−N)=0, while φ*−φ=2x>0. KL therefore fails. The Example verifies KL only for x∈[1,2] and only on a fixed sublevel set, so the claim that it satisfies the paper's local KL assumption is unsupported. The same objection applies to the numerical test problem, where no check of the assumption is given. The advertised generality (a local KL condition that avoids a global one) does not match what the assumption actually demands.

failure_location.quote: For example, the minimax problem in Example~\eqref{example} satisfies the local KL condition but not the global one.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Impose the KL condition only for x∈𝒳 (or for x∈Ω with ∂Ψ(x)≠∅), or choose a different convention outside 𝒳. Then re-check that 𝒰_ε, its openness (Lemma lem:open), and the use of Ω in Theorem thm:Phi_smooth remain valid, for instance by taking 𝒰_ε as a relatively open subset of 𝒳.
issues.overall_effect: The motivating example and the claimed advantage over global-KL settings are not covered by the stated assumption. Theorems that rely on Assumption (iii) on all of Ω (including the definition and openness of 𝒰_ε) are proved for a class that excludes the paper's own example.
issues.title: Assumption (iii) with dist(0,∅)=∞ forces a global KL condition outside dom p, so the Example/Remark claim of local-KL validity fails
issues.why_classification: The fix is a contained change to the assumption and to the definition and openness of 𝒰_ε, with a re-check of how Ω is used. The main method and rates survive.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: the proximal operators of $p$ and $q$ can be computed exactly
the number of evaluations of the proximal operator $p$ equals the number of iterations

issues.failure_explanation: Each outer iteration solves min over x∈B(x^k,r) of ⟨g,x⟩+(L_k/2)‖x−x^k‖²+p(x). This is the prox of p+I_{B(x^k,r)}, not the prox of p. For general closed convex p, the ball-constrained prox cannot be obtained from prox_p in finitely many exact evaluations. For example, in the numerical problem p already contains an indicator of the unit ball plus an ℓ1 term, so the new feasible set is an intersection of two balls. Assumption (ii) grants only exact prox_p and prox_q. The algorithm's step therefore relies on an oracle that is not assumed, and the stated count 'number of prox_p evaluations = number of iterations' is unsupported. The ball constraint is essential to the analysis, because it keeps the Hölder bound valid and the step length at most r.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Either assume an exact oracle for prox of p+I_{B(x^k,r)} and count that oracle, or show how to compute the ball-constrained prox from prox_p (for example with a 1D root-finding or dual argument) and bound its additional cost.
issues.overall_effect: The oracle-complexity accounting for p, and the claim that only prox evaluations of p and q and gradients of f are needed, do not follow under the stated assumptions. The iteration bound in thm:outer_bound is unaffected.
issues.title: Outer step is a ball-constrained prox subproblem but is counted as one evaluation of prox_p, which Assumption (ii) does not provide
issues.why_classification: Convergence analysis and iteration complexity are untouched. The repair is a clarified oracle assumption or a contained subroutine plus a cost bound, which leaves the results comparable.
